L7@P0: Abstract. The pop-stack operator of a finite lattice L is the map that sends each x in L to
L8@P0: the meet of x with the set of elements covered by x. Using tools from representation
L9@P0: theory, we provide simple Coxeter-theoretic and lattice-theoretic descriptions of the
L10@P0: image of the pop-stack operator of a Cambrian lattice of a finite irreducible Coxeter
L11@P0: group. When specialized to a bipartite Cambrian lattice of type A, this result settles a
L12@P0: conjecture of Choi and Sun. We also settle a related enumerative conjecture of Defant
L13@P0: and Williams. When L is an arbitrary lattice quotient of the weak order on W, we
L14@P0: prove that the maximum size of a forward orbit under the pop-stack operator of L is
L15@P0: at most the Coxeter number of W; when L is a Cambrian lattice, we provide an explicit
L16@P0: construction to show that this maximum forward orbit size is actually equal to the
L17@P0: Coxeter number.
L18@P0: Keywords: torsion classes, Cambrian lattice, weak order, pop-stack operator

L85@P1: Given an interesting lattice L, one of the primary problems one can consider about
L86@P1: its pop-stack operator is that of maximizing OL(x). When L is the weak order on a
L87@P1: finite irreducible Coxeter group W, Defant [7] proved that maxx∈L |OL(x)| is the Coxeter
L88@P1: number h of W; in type A, this result was originally proven much earlier by Ungar [17].
L89@P1: Defant also studied this problem for ν-Tamari lattices in [6].
L90@P1: Defant and Williams [8] found that it is fruitful to study the image of the pop-stack
L91@P1: operator when L is a semidistributive (or more generally, a semidistrim) lattice; this is
L92@P1: because the image of pop↓ has numerous interesting properties, some of which relate to
L93@P1: a certain bijective rowmotion operator row: L → L. For example, |pop↓(L)| and |pop↑(L)|
L94@P1: are both equal to the number of elements x ∈ L such that row(x) ≤ x. The images of
L95@P1: pop↓ and pop↑ are also naturally in bijection with the set of facets of a certain simplicial
L96@P1: complex called the canonical join complex of L.

L15@P0: Flips of diagonals in colored triangle-free triangulations of a convex polygon are
L16@P0: interpreted as moves between two adjacent chambers in a certain graphic hyperplane
L17@P0: arrangement. Properties of geodesics in the associated flip graph are deduced. In
L18@P0: particular, it is shown that: (1) every diagonal is flipped exactly once in a geodesic
L19@P0: between distinguished pairs of antipodes; (2) the number of geodesics between these
L20@P0: antipodes is equal to twice the number of standard Young tableaux of a truncated
L21@P0: shifted staircase shape.
L22@P0: 1 Introduction
L23@P0: It was shown in [1] that the diameter of the flip graph on the set of all colored triangle-free
L24@P0: triangulations of a convex n-gon (to be defined in Subsection 2.1) is exactly n(n − 3)/2.
L25@P0: Observing that this is the number of diagonals in a convex n-gon, it was conjectured by
L26@P0: Richard Stanley that all diagonals are flipped in a geodesic between two antipodes.
L27@P0: In this paper Stanley’s conjecture is proved for distinguished pairs of antipodes (Corollary 5.3 below). The proof applies a Cen-action on arc permutations, which yields an
L28@P0: embedding of the flip graph in a graphic hyperplane arrangement. Geodesics between
L29@P0: distinguished antipodes in the flip graph are then interpreted as minimal galleries from a
L30@P0: given chamber c to the negative chamber −c, while diagonals are interpreted as separating
L31@P0: hyperplanes.
L32@P0: ∗Research of both authors was supported in part by an internal grant from Bar-Ilan University.

L38@P1: 2 Triangle-Free Triangulations
L39@P1: In this Section we recall basic concepts and main results from [1].
L40@P1: 2.1 Basic Concepts
L41@P1: Label the vertices of a convex n-gon Pn (n > 4) by the elements 0, . . . , n−1 of the additive
L42@P1: cyclic group Zn. Consider a triangulation (with no extra vertices) of the polygon. Each
L43@P1: edge of the polygon is called an external edge of the triangulation; all other edges of the
L44@P1: triangulation are called internal edges, or chords.
L45@P1: Definition 2.1 A triangulation of a convex n-gon Pn is called internal-triangle-free, or
L46@P1: simply triangle-free, if it contains no triangle with 3 internal edges. The set of all trianglefree triangulations of Pn is denoted T F T(n).
L47@P1: A chord in Pn is called short if it connects the vertices labeled i−1 and i+ 1, for some
L48@P1: i ∈ Zn. A triangulation is triangle-free if and only if it contains only two short chords [1,
L49@P1: Claim 2.3].
L50@P1: A proper coloring (or orientation) of a triangulation T ∈ T F T(n) is a labeling of the
L51@P1: chords by 0, . . . , n − 4 such that
L52@P1: 1. One of the short chords is labeled 0.
L53@P1: 2. If a triangle has exactly two internal edges then their labels are consective integers
L54@P1: i, i + 1.
L55@P1: It is easy to see that each T ∈ T F T(n) has exactly two proper colorings. The set of all
L56@P1: properly colored triangle-free triangulations is denoted CT F T(n).
L57@P1: Each chord in a triangulation is a diagonal of a unique quadrangle (the union of two
L58@P1: adjacent triangles). Replacing this chord by the other diagonal of that quadrangle is a flip
L59@P1: of the chord. A flip in a colored triangulation preserves the color of the flipped diagonal.
L60@P1: Definition 2.2 The colored flip graph Γn is defined as follows: the vertices are all the
L61@P1: colored triangle-free triangulations in CT F T(n). Two triangulations are connected in Γn
L62@P1: by an edge labeled i if one is obtained from the other by a flip of the chord labeled i.
L63@P1: See Figure 2.1 for a drawing of Γ7, where the coloring of a triangulation is displayed
L64@P1: by shading the triangle with the short chord labeled 0 and two external edges as sides.
